metadata.title: Gender inequality and adolescent bullying victimization among 69 countries and its effect modification by corporal punishment prohibiting laws

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students and applies OECD Balanced Repeated Replication (BRR) weights to account for the complex two-stage stratified and clustered sampling design (schools sampled with probability proportional to size, then students within schools). The analytic sample is restricted to 69 eligible countries/economies after excluding subsamples with missing country-level gender inequality indices and excluding students with missing victimization data; additionally, students were retained if they answered at least five of six victimization items. Missingness in one victimization item (2.3%) was handled via person-mean imputation rather than listwise deletion. The paper does not report any ML-specific omission of weights; instead, it explicitly states that all multilevel models used BRR weights to adjust for complex survey design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is a composite victimization frequency score derived from six self-report items (range 6–24), not a PV-based cognitive achievement scale. Missing data handling is reported: participants were included if they responded to at least five of six items, and the single missing bullying item (2.3%) was imputed using person-mean imputation. Therefore, the study does not require PV generation/combining rules.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 nationally representative cross-sectional data for 15-year-old students. Excluded five PISA subsamples (“economies”), four countries/territories due to missing country-level gender inequality indices (2018 GII), and four countries due to missing victimization data. For the victimization composite, included participants who responded to at least five of six victimization questions to avoid bias from listwise deletion; the remaining missing bullying item (2.3%) was imputed using person-mean imputation. The final analytic sample comprises 433,836 students from 69 eligible countries.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) victimization composite score (verbal/physical/relational) across 69 countries
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear regression (3-level: students within schools within countries). Country-level variance explained: ICC country variance 5.9% (Model 0). GII effect per 1 SD increase: b=0.52 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.73) in Model 1; interaction GII*sex: b=-0.23 (95% CI -0.32 to -0.14) in Model 2. Law modification: full ban ≤10y vs no/partial ban b=-0.43 (95% CI -0.75 to -0.10) in Model 3; full ban >10y b=0.12 (95% CI -0.32 to 0.56). Robustness: effects remained after adjusting for covariates (Model 5) and anti-bullying policy (Model 6).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged gender inequality index (GII), sex, and national corporal punishment ban status (plus socioeconomic status and gender equality knowledge) to model total victimization score, finding that higher country-level gender inequality was associated with higher victimization and that this association was stronger for boys. This indicates that gender-inequality-focused prevention and gender-norm transformation may be important for reducing adolescent bullying victimization, while recent national corporal punishment prohibitions may attenuate the gender inequality–victimization link (causality cannot be inferred due to cross-sectional ecological design).

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzed PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students across 69 eligible countries to explain cross-country differences in adolescent bullying victimization. The outcome was a composite total victimization score (6–24) based on six self-report items covering verbal, physical, and relational victimization over the past 12 months; one missing item (2.3%) was imputed using person-mean imputation, and students were included if they answered at least five of six items. Using three-level multilevel linear regression (students within schools within countries) with OECD BRR weights, the authors found that higher country-level gender inequality (GII) predicted higher victimization (b=0.52 per 1 SD GII; 95% CI 0.32–0.73), with a stronger association for boys (GII*sex b=-0.23). National laws fully prohibiting corporal punishment enacted within the past 10 years significantly attenuated the GII–victimization association (b=-0.43), while bans enacted for >10 years did not. Limitations include cross-sectional design (no causal inference) and ecological fallacy risk, plus restricted country coverage (PISA excludes low-income/African countries).
data.null_fields_interpretation: Although the Scopus catalog suggests an AI/ML theme, the paper does not train or evaluate any machine learning models; it uses multilevel linear regression with survey-weighted estimation. Therefore, ML technique fields are intentionally empty and plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variable is a non-PV composite victimization score.
